body.statement: Let \(P\) be homogeneous of degree \(r\geq1\). If \(G_P(X)\succeq0\) for every \(X\in C3\), \(\det G_P\equiv0\) in \(\mathbb R[S3]\), and \(\operatorname{rank}G_P(X_0)=2\) for some \(X_0\in C3\), then there exists \(u\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(G_P(X)u=0\) identically on \(S3\). Consequently, after a linear change of coordinates, \(P\) is a polynomial in one \(2\times2\) symmetric compression of \(X\).
body.justification: Adjugate-ray invariance and two-sided Loewner comparison force a global kernel without degree or nonresonance restrictions.
body.gap: The hypothesis \(\det G_P\equiv0\) is determinant singularity of the \(3\times3\) symmetric-gradient matrix, not vanishing of a six-coordinate Hessian determinant; the coordinate-Hessian literature therefore cannot yield this conclusion.
body.consumer: The complete denominator classification applies this theorem to the signed mixed residue supplied by Lemma 3.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(G=G_P\).  We first derive monotonicity from the positive-semidefinite gradient hypothesis.  If \(A,B\in C3\) and \(B-A\succeq0\), convexity of \(C3\) and the fundamental theorem of calculus give
\[
 P(B)-P(A)
 =\int_0^1\operatorname{tr}\!\left(G(A+s(B-A))(B-A)\right)\,\mathrm ds\geq0. \tag{4}
\]
The last inequality holds because the trace of the product of two positive-semidefinite symmetric matrices is nonnegative.

Choose \(X_0\in C3\) with \(\operatorname{rank}G(X_0)=2\).  Since \(G(X_0)\succeq0\), its two nonzero eigenvalues are positive.  Consequently
\[
 Q_P(X_0)=\operatorname{adj}G(X_0)=\kappa uu^{\top}
\]
for some \(\kappa>0\) and some \(u\neq0\) spanning \(\ker G(X_0)\).  The adjugate-translation lemma, followed by rescaling its scalar parameter by \(\kappa\), gives
\[
 P(X_0+tuu^{\top})=P(X_0) \qquad(t\in\mathbb R). \tag{5}
\]

Fix arbitrary \(X\in C3\).  Because \(X_0\succ0\), there is \(R>0\) such that \(X\preceq RX_0\); for example, any \(R\) not smaller than the largest eigenvalue of \(X_0^{-1/2}XX_0^{-1/2}\) works.  For every \(t\geq0\), all matrices in the following comparison are positive definite.  Applying (4), homogeneity of degree \(r\), and (5), in that order, gives the two-sided bound
\[
 P(X)
 \leq P(X+tuu^{\top})
 \leq P(RX_0+tuu^{\top})
 =R^rP\!\left(X_0+\frac{t}{R}uu^{\top}\right)
 =R^rP(X_0). \tag{6}
\]
Thus the real polynomial \(t\mapsto P(X+tuu^{\top})\) is bounded above and below on \([0,\infty)\).  A nonconstant real polynomial is unbounded in absolute value on that half-line, so this polynomial is constant.  Differentiating at \(t=0\) gives
\[
 u^{\top}G(X)u=0.
\]
Since \(G(X)\succeq0\), the spectral theorem implies \(G(X)u=0\).  This holds for every \(X\in C3\).  Each coordinate of the vector-valued polynomial \(G(X)u\) vanishes on the nonempty open set \(C3\), hence vanishes identically on \(S3\).

Finally choose an invertible, and in fact orthogonal, change of coordinates carrying \(u\) to a nonzero multiple of the third coordinate vector.  Then \(G(X)u=0\) says that the derivatives of \(P\) with respect to \(x_{13},x_{23},x_{33}\) vanish; the off-diagonal equalities use the half-weighted gradient convention.  A polynomial with these three zero partial derivatives depends only on \(x_{11},x_{12},x_{22}\), namely on the symmetric compression of \(X\) to \(u^{\perp}\).  This proves both conclusions.
